Let me check the detail field: "Several of our distribution operator customers carry out dissolved gas analysis on their oil-filled transformers every one to two years and record the results in maintenance logs. They also have load data from SCADA — hourly active power readings going back between three and eight years depending on the operator. What they do not have is any way to turn those two sources into a ranked list of transformers most likely to fail in the next twelve months."

So the quote "no way to turn those two sources into a ranked list of transformers most likely to fail in the next twelve months" should be in there. The fact checker says "quote not found" - maybe there's a subtle difference. Let me reread... 

The confirming quote is there, but I'm realizing the number "every one to two years" also needs its own supporting citation, so I should pull that phrase in as a second quote alongside the "no way to turn" quote.

For the other claims, I'm checking which record fields actually back them up — the four hundred transformers figure maps cleanly, but the engineer and Azure infrastructure details come from different parts of the term sheet versus the operational records, so I need to split the sourcing accordingly rather than treating them as one unified citation.

For claim four, I found the right quote: "achieves a fault-prediction horizon of up to six months before confirmed failure" from the abstract. For claim five, I need to locate quotes confirming the researcher led ML model design for DGA and load prediction, likely from the bio or the same publication.

Now I'm piecing together claim one, which needs two sources: one confirming the "every one to two years" cadence for dissolved gas analysis and another confirming the lack of a ranked failure list. I'm drafting the sentence combining both quotes, but I need to double-check that "every one to two years" appears verbatim in the source text before finalizing it.

For claim two, I'll use the quote about four hundred transformers across two operators with failure event records. For claim three, I'm wrestling with how to phrase the company's Azure contribution without overstating it -- the source only lists specific Azure services, not that they're used for "model training and hosting," so I need a more cautious phrasing that sticks closer to what's actually documented.

I'll drop claim three entirely since no record fully supports it. For claim four, I'll pull directly from the SYN-PUB-07733 abstract, citing the ML framework combining dissolved gas analysis with historical load profiles and the six-month fault-prediction horizon. For claim five, I'm matching the researcher's ML model design role with the company's GridSense Assets integration work, pulling from the relevant bio and term sheet details.

Now I'm working through claim one more carefully, checking whether the specific quote about turning DGA and SCADA data into a ranked failure list is actually supported in the source record, since the fact checker flagged that the exact phrasing with "next twelve months" wasn't found. I need to look again at the detail text to see what's actually there.

I settle on dropping claim three since there isn't solid record support linking the engineer and Azure together, and finalize the remaining claims with their sources: the four-hundred-transformer dataset, the published ML framework for DGA and load-based failure prediction, and the division of labor between the researcher's model work and the engineering team's integration into GridSense Assets. With sources confirmed, I'm ready to compile the final JSON.
